Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that truth-value directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: Massive Activations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are massive activations in large language models and vision transformers, where are they located, and what functional role do they serve?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers and analyzes massive activations in LLMs and ViTs, showing they act as input-agnostic bias terms that concentrate attention and can be eliminated by augmenting self-attention with explicit biases.
papers.conclusion: Massive activations are a widespread phenomenon in large Transformers that act as implicit biases in attention computation, and they can be removed by using explicit attention biases.
papers.key_findings:
Massive activations (extremely large activation values) are widespread in LLMs and ViTs.
They are input-agnostic and function as crucial, fixed bias terms in the models.
They cause attention to concentrate on the tokens where they appear.
Explicitly adding bias terms to self-attention eliminates the need for massive activations.
In ViTs, register tokens function similarly as learned biases.
papers.limitation: Experiments with the new attention formulation were limited to a small GPT-2 model due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Investigate how instruction fine-tuning affects massive activations.
Study how the BOS token affects the positions of massive activations.
Generalize results to larger models and study the training stability of the new attention formulation.
papers.abstract: We observe an empirical phenomenon in Large Language Models (LLMs) -- very few activations exhibit significantly larger values than others (e.g., 100,000 times larger). We call them massive activations. First, we demonstrate the widespread existence of massive activations across various LLMs and characterize their locations. Second, we find their values largely stay constant regardless of the input, and they function as indispensable bias terms in LLMs. Third, these massive activations lead to the concentration of attention probabilities to their corresponding tokens, and further, implicit bias terms in the self-attention output. Last, we also study massive activations in Vision Transformers. Code is available at https://github.com/locuslab/massive-activations.

papers.title: Do You Trust Me? Cognitive-Affective Signatures of Trustworthiness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do instruction-tuned LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in narratives, where do these representations emerge across transformer depth, how well can they be decoded, and how do they relate to psychological constructs like fairness and certainty?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in systematic, layer- and head-specific patterns that are linearly decodable and align with psychological constructs like fairness and certainty, demonstrating that trust signals emerge during pretraining without explicit supervision.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals, offering a representational foundation for designing credible and trustworthy AI systems in web applications.
papers.key_findings:
Activation differences between high- and low-trust narratives are observed across models, indicating trust-sensitive features emerge during pretraining.
Trustworthiness is linearly decodable from intermediate representations, with probe performance varying by layer and head.
Fine-tuning with LoRA sharpens existing trust representations rather than restructuring them.
Trust representations are most strongly associated with psychological appraisals like fairness, certainty, and accountability-self.
Nonlinear probes provide only marginal gains, indicating trust information is largely in linearly accessible subspaces.
papers.abstract: Perceived trustworthiness underpins how users navigate online information, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs),increasingly embedded in search, recommendation, and conversational systems, represent this construct in psychologically coherent ways. We analyze how instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Mistral 7B) encode perceived trustworthiness in web-like narratives using the PEACE-Reviews dataset annotated for cognitive appraisals, emotions, and behavioral intentions. Across models, systematic layer- and head-level activation differences distinguish high- from low-trust texts, revealing that trust cues are implicitly encoded during pretraining. Probing analyses show linearly de-codable trust signals and fine-tuning effects that refine rather than restructure these representations. Strongest associations emerge with appraisals of fairness, certainty, and accountability-self -- dimensions central to human trust formation online. These findings demonstrate that modern LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals without explicit supervision, offering a representational foundation for designing credible, transparent, and trust-worthy AI systems in the web ecosystem. Code and appendix are available at: https://github.com/GerardYeo/TrustworthinessLLM.

papers.title: Analysing Moral Bias in Finetuned LLMs through Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (a moral bias in intentionality judgments), whether specific Transformer layers encode this bias, and whether targeted interventions (layer-patching) can mitigate it.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the Knobe effect (a moral bias) emerges in finetuned LLMs, is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, and can be mitigated by patching activations from pretrained models into finetuned models, without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that social biases in LLMs can be mechanistically localized and mitigated through targeted interventions like layer-patching, offering a method for model repair without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Finetuned LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (moral bias in intentionality judgments), while pretrained models show minimal effect.
The bias is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, as shown by differences in residual stream activations.
Patching activations from pretrained models into specific layers of finetuned models can reduce or eliminate the bias.
The mitigation via layer-patching does not significantly harm general model performance on standard benchmarks.
The Knobe effect is not an emergent property of model scale alone; it is induced by finetuning and appears across model sizes.
papers.limitation: The layer-patching method requires access to the pretrained model.
future_direction: Explore whether this localization technique applies to other biases, such as gender or racial stereotypes.
Develop methods that do not rely on access to the pretrained model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to internalize human-like biases during finetuning, yet the mechanisms by which these biases manifest remain unclear. In this work, we investigated whether the well-known Knobe effect, a moral bias in intentionality judgements, emerges in finetuned LLMs and whether it can be traced back to specific components of the model. We conducted a Layer-Patching analysis across 3 open-weights LLMs and demonstrated that the bias is not only learned during finetuning but also localized in a specific set of layers. Surprisingly, we found that patching activations from the corresponding pretrained model into just a few critical layers is sufficient to eliminate the effect. Our findings offer new evidence that social biases in LLMs can be interpreted, localized, and mitigated through targeted interventions, without the need for model retraining.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: Investigating a neural language model’s replicability of psycholinguistic experiments: A case study of NPI licensing
papers.research_question: Does the neural language model BERT capture syntactic and semantic constraints in Negative Polarity Item (NPI) processing, and does it exhibit processing patterns (including grammatical illusion) similar to humans?
papers.core_contribution: The neural language model BERT is highly sensitive to both syntactic and semantic constraints in NPI processing, and its processing patterns and sensitivities are very close to humans, suggesting its role as a research tool or object in the study of language.
papers.conclusion: BERT exhibits knowledge necessary for processing linguistic input and returns results analogous to human language comprehension, suggesting it can be a testable toolset for linguists and psycholinguists.
papers.key_findings:
BERT successfully discriminates between syntactically correct and incorrect licensor positions for NPIs.
BERT shows susceptibility to grammatical illusion, analogous to human processing errors.
BERT distinguishes between licensors of different semantic strengths (e.g., classic negation 'no' vs. minimal negation 'few').
BERT's evaluation of the licensor 'only' yielded inconsistent results depending on the measurement position (NPI vs. licensor).
Overall, BERT's behavior in NPI processing closely mirrors human psycholinguistic patterns.
papers.limitation:
BERT is bidirectional, which differs from the unidirectional, incremental nature of human sentence processing, making direct comparison of surprisal values problematic.
Inconsistent results for the licensor 'only' depending on the mask position (NPI vs. licensor) indicate complexity in modeling its semantic/pragmatic behavior.
future_direction: Investigate how the transiency and the medium degree of surprisal in BERT's illusion effect are analogous to human processing.
Use BERT for crosslinguistic comparisons, e.g., between retrospective licensing languages (like English) and prospective licensing languages (like Korean).
papers.abstract: The recent success of deep learning neural language models such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) has brought innovations to computational language research. The present study explores the possibility of using a language model in investigating human language processes, based on the case study of negative polarity items (NPIs). We first conducted an experiment with BERT to examine whether the model successfully captures the hierarchical structural relationship between an NPI and its licensor and whether it may lead to an error analogous to the grammatical illusion shown in the psycholinguistic experiment (Experiment 1). We also investigated whether the language model can capture the fine-grained semantic properties of NPI licensors and discriminate their subtle differences on the scale of licensing strengths (Experiment 2). The results of the two experiments suggest that overall, the neural language model is highly sensitive to both syntactic and semantic constraints in NPI processing. The model's processing patterns and sensitivities are shown to be very close to humans, suggesting their role as a research tool or object in the study of language.

papers.title: Ungrammatical Influences: Evidence for Dynamical Language Processing
papers.research_question: Do ungrammatical influences exist in human sentence processing? Specifically, are readers temporarily distracted by coherent but grammatically incompatible local structures during parsing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence from a connectionist model and human reading experiments that ungrammatical local structures can influence parsing, supporting a dynamical, self-organizing approach to language processing.
papers.conclusion: Ungrammatical influences exist in human sentence processing, and dynamical, self-organizing models like connectionist networks can account for these effects, pointing towards parallel processing solutions to parsing tractability.
papers.key_findings:
A Simple Recurrent Network model shows higher error (Kullback-Leibler Divergence) on sentences containing irrelevant local coherences (e.g., noun-noun compounds) that are grammatically incompatible with the global structure.
Human reading times are slower for sentences containing such ungrammatical local coherences (Experiment 1), indicating distraction by grammatically ruled-out interpretations.
A stronger slowing effect is found for reduced relative clauses with homophonous verbs compared to non-homophonous verbs (Experiment 2), showing the effect extends beyond lexical compounds.
The results suggest that parsing involves competition among local coherences via dynamical feedback, rather than deductive elimination of parses based on top-down constraints.
The connectionist model's behavior aligns with human data, indicating that dynamical, self-organizing mechanisms may address tractability problems in parsing.
papers.limitation:
The effect in the network simulation was somewhat unstable with longer training on the same materials and sometimes reversed itself.
Experiment 1 results could be explained by lexical automaticity (activation of compound senses in the lexicon) rather than syntactic parsing interference, though Experiment 2 addresses this.
future_direction: Further exploration of dynamical parsing models that use feedback and self-organization to handle incoherent structure representation.
Incorporating the problem of incoherent structure representation into the theory of grammar.
papers.abstract: Ungrammatical Inuences: Evidence for Dynamical Language Processing Whitney Tabor tabor@uconnvm.uconn.edu Bruno Galantucci Bruno.Galantucci@uconn.edu Department of Psychology University of Connecticut Storrs, CT 06269 USA Abstract A distinguishing feature of self-organizing models of cog- nitive structure is that they permit incompatible struc- tures to coexist at least temporarily. Here we report on a connectionist model of natural language process- ing which appears to temporarily construct incoherent structures. We then describe two reading-time studies which reveal people exhibiting the same tendency. In particular, both networks and people show sensitivity to the irrelevant structural interpretations of the under- lined phrases in (1) and (2). (1) We did not think the company would re truck drivers without consulting the union rst. (2) The manager watched the waiter served pea soup by the trainee. This kind of sensitivity is absent in parsing models which treat grammatical constraints as absolute because such models lack a principled method of generating incoher- ent parses. Connectionist networks make the right pre- dictions by using feedback and self-organization. Our results push in the direction of seeking a solution to the tractability problems of parsing by using dynamical mechanisms in a parallel architecture. Introduction Current sentence-processing research tends to focus on ambiguity-related processing in sentences like (1) { (3): (1) The mechanic maintained the truck was working beautifully. (2) The cop arrested by the detective was chagrined. (3) The cook stirred the soup with the tomatoes. Each of these sentences has a structural ambiguity which is resolved on the basis of structural or pragmatic infor- mation when the underlined words arrive. Reading time and eye tracking studies show that when biases favor the wrong interpretation initially, readers tend to slow down and/or make regressions in the disambiguating re- gion, which suggests that they either choose the wrong parse initially or are biased toward it (see Frazier, 1988; Tanenhaus & Trueswell, 1995). Such phenomena accord well with a model of sen- tence processing which assumes people construct phrase- structure parses incrementally based on the input up to the current point in time. On this view, the slow-down in the disambiguating region is due either to extra time Figure 1: The Zollner illusion. spent on revising an incorrect parse, or to extra time spent on revising the weighting assigned to dierent pos- sible parses maintained in parallel. Focusing for a moment on cognitive processes outside of sentence processing, there is a good deal of evidence that people are reliably vulnerable to certain adverse inuences when interpreting complex stimuli. In the Zollner illusion (Held, 1971|Figure 1), lines on a page appear to be nonparallel even though retinal and depth of eld information indicate parallelism. Similarly, in the Stroop eect (Stroop, 1966), a decision is supposed to have been made ahead of time to interpret the stimulus along one particular dimension of contrast (e.g. color), and yet when the stimulus is presented, people are often led astray by irrelevant verbal information. These cases are dierent from the classic sentence pro- cessing examples listed in (1) through (3) in that they show people temporarily failing to rule out an interpre- tation that could be ruled out absolutely, given the in- formation at hand. What would be the analogous cases in sentence processing? Denition of Ungrammatical Inuences There is a class of sentences in which one parse of a word sequence can be completely ruled out on grammatical grounds and yet (we hypothesize) people are inuenced by it anyway. The following are examples of such hy- pothesized \Ungrammatical Inuences : (4) a. They won't re truck drivers on Sunday. b. They won't hire truck drivers on Sunday.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: From Black Boxes to Transparent Minds: Evaluating and Enhancing the Theory of Mind in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate and enhance Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from an interpretability perspective?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GridToM, a novel multimodal dataset for evaluating Theory of Mind (ToM), analyzes internal attention representations in MLLMs to show they distinguish perspective information, and proposes a training-free intervention method that enhances ToM performance by shifting activations along specific attention head directions.
papers.conclusion: The analysis of internal mechanisms shows that MLLMs develop attention heads capable of distinguishing perspective information and reasoning about beliefs, and targeted interventions based on these representations can significantly enhance their exhibited Theory of Mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in multimodal large language models can distinguish cognitive information across different perspectives, providing evidence of internal Theory of Mind representations.
A training-free intervention method, which adjusts activations in the direction of sensitive attention heads, significantly improves model performance on first-order and second-order belief tasks.
Multimodal large language models perform better on text-based ToM tasks compared to video-only tasks.
Linear probing reveals that belief states are linearly separable in the activation space of attention heads, indicating structured internal representations.
The constructed GridToM dataset enables comprehensive and interpretability-driven evaluation of ToM capabilities in MLLMs.
papers.limitation:
The tasks in the dataset are limited to first-order and second-order belief tasks within the ATOMs framework, while ToM theory encompasses a broader range of unexplored tasks.
Due to restrictions in accessing model code, the approach was only validated on a limited selection of MLLMs.
papers.abstract: As large language models evolve, there is growing anticipation that they will emulate human-like Theory of Mind (ToM) to assist with routine tasks. However, existing methods for evaluating machine ToM focus primarily on unimodal models and largely treat these models as black boxes, lacking an interpretative exploration of their internal mechanisms. In response, this study adopts an approach based on internal mechanisms to provide an interpretability-driven assessment of ToM in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Specifically, we first construct a multimodal ToM test dataset, GridToM, which incorporates diverse belief testing tasks and perceptual information from multiple perspectives. Next, our analysis shows that attention heads in multimodal large models can distinguish cognitive information across perspectives, providing evidence of ToM capabilities. Furthermore, we present a lightweight, training-free approach that significantly enhances the model's exhibited ToM by adjusting in the direction of the attention head.

papers.title: Counterfactual reasoning: an analysis of in-context emergence
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning, i.e., predicting consequences of hypothetical scenarios by inferring unobserved latent concepts and copying contextual noise from factual observations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models are capable of in-context counterfactual reasoning, and through analysis of Transformers, finds that self-attention, model depth, and pre-training data diversity drive performance, with mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and that designated noise abduction heads emerge.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can perform counterfactual reasoning by leveraging self-attention and depth, and this ability extends to sequential data, suggesting potential for counterfactual story generation.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning on synthetic linear regression tasks.
Self-attention is crucial for counterfactual reasoning; MLP-only models fail.
Model depth improves counterfactual reasoning performance.
Pre-training data diversity improves performance and out-of-distribution generalization.
The latent parameter is linearly encoded in the residual stream, and designated noise abduction heads emerge in attention layers.
papers.limitation: The synthetic setup may not fully capture the complexity of natural language counterfactual reasoning.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to natural language tasks and more complex functions.
Further exploration of the role of attention heads in counterfactual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit remarkable performance in in-context learning: the ability to learn and reason about the input context on the fly. This work studies in-context counterfactual reasoning in language models, that is, the ability to predict consequences of a hypothetical scenario. We focus on a well-defined, synthetic linear regression task that requires noise abduction. Accurate prediction is based on (1) inferring an unobserved latent concept and (2) copying contextual noise from factual observations. We show that language models are capable of counterfactual reasoning. Further, we enhance existing identifiability results and reduce counterfactual reasoning for a broad class of functions to a transformation on in-context observations. In Transformers, we find that self-attention, model depth and pre-training data diversity drive performance. Moreover, we provide mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and we introduce designated \textit{noise abduction heads} central to performing counterfactual reasoning. Lastly, our findings extend to counterfactual reasoning under SDE dynamics and reflect that Transformers can perform noise abduction on sequential data, providing preliminary evidence on the potential for counterfactual story generation. Our code is available under https://github.com/mrtzmllr/iccr.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Calibrating LLM Confidence by Probing Perturbed Representation Stability
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM confidence estimation by analyzing the stability of internal representations under targeted adversarial perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CCPS, a method that estimates LLM confidence by analyzing the stability of internal representations under adversarial perturbations, achieving significant improvements in calibration and discrimination metrics across diverse models and benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CCPS provides an efficient, accurate, and generalizable method for LLM confidence estimation, enhancing the trustworthiness of LLMs in critical domains.
papers.key_findings:
CCPS reduces average Expected Calibration Error by approximately 55% (up to 88%) and Brier score by 21% (up to 45%) compared to the best baseline.
CCPS increases average Accuracy by 5 percentage points, AUCPR by 4 percentage points, and AUROC by 6 percentage points.
CCPS generalizes across diverse LLM architectures (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) and model scales (8B to 32B parameters).
CCPS performs well on both multiple-choice and open-ended question answering formats.
CCPS is parameter-efficient, adding only around 9.5k trainable parameters, compared to baselines that may add millions.
papers.abstract: Reza Khanmohammadi, Erfan Miahi, Mehrsa Mardikoraem, Simerjot Kaur, Ivan Brugere, Charese Smiley, Kundan S Thind, Mohammad M. Ghassemi. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Steering Risk Preferences in Large Language Models by Aligning Behavioral and Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors be systematically identified to change LLM behavior? The paper proposes a principled approach by aligning latent representations from behavioral methods (Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with neural counterparts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for deriving steering vectors by aligning behavioral representations (elicited via MCMC with LLMs) with neural activations, enabling precise control of LLM risk preferences without retraining.
papers.conclusion: Self-alignment methods that align behavioral and neural representations offer an effective and principled means of controlling LLM behavior in risk-sensitive contexts.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors derived from aligned behavioral and neural representations (MCMC and Certainty Equivalent methods) outperform Contrastive Activation in steering risky decisions, risk perception, and text generation.
The optimal layer for steering varies: risk perception is more steerable in earlier layers, while risky decisions are more steerable in later layers.
The method allows precise control over risk preferences (risk-seeking vs. risk-averse) across different tasks.
Steering vectors transfer to tasks far from the original elicitation context.
The behavioral representation from MCMC reveals more nuanced risk preferences compared to the Certainty Equivalent method.
papers.limitation:
Further theoretical and mechanistic interpretability research is needed to establish a more concrete link between behaviorally elicited representations and their corresponding neural activations.
Modifying a Transformer’s residual stream is not uniformly effective across all layers; the success of such interventions is highly dependent on the layer selected. Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question.
This form of steering is limited in scope for proprietary models where weights are not accessible, restricting its broader applicability.
future_direction: Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question for future research.
Future research should consider developing new descriptive frameworks tailored to characterizing and predicting the risky choices of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Changing the behavior of large language models (LLMs) can be as straightforward as editing the Transformer's residual streams using appropriately constructed "steering vectors." These modifications to internal neural activations, a form of representation engineering, offer an effective and targeted means of influencing model behavior without retraining or fine-tuning the model. But how can such steering vectors be systematically identified? We propose a principled approach for uncovering steering vectors by aligning latent representations elicited through behavioral methods (specifically, Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with their neural counterparts. To evaluate this approach, we focus on extracting latent risk preferences from LLMs and steering their risk-related outputs using the aligned representations as steering vectors. We show that the resulting steering vectors successfully and reliably modulate LLM outputs in line with the targeted behavior.

papers.title: Universal and Independent: Multilingual Probing Framework for Exhaustive Model Interpretation and Evaluation
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether linguistic regularities detected by probing are coherent across typologically diverse languages, and it aims to provide a framework for exhaustive multilingual probing of language models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a framework for exhaustive multilingual probing of language models, using Universal Dependencies data, and applies it to mBERT and XLM-R, showing that mBERT performs better on Standard Average European languages and that script does not impact performance but language family does.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents the Universal Probing framework for multilingual probing, which can be used for model interpretation and evaluation, and hopes it will lead to better and more explainable NLP.
papers.key_findings:
The framework allows probing of 104 languages and 80 morphosyntactic features.
mBERT and XLM-R perform similarly on average, but mBERT is slightly better.
Models perform better on high-resource languages and worse on under-resourced non-Indo-European languages.
Performance is correlated with language family but not with script.
Models are biased towards Standard Average European (SAE) languages, performing better on categories found in SAE languages.
papers.limitation:
The framework depends on the quality and consistency of Universal Dependencies data, which may contain annotation errors and version instability.
The framework allows the use of various probing methods, including those that are widely criticized, so researchers must choose methods carefully.
future_direction: Including syntactic markup in research
Developing an interface with a CQL-like query language for creating custom probing tasks
papers.abstract: Linguistic analysis of language models is one of the ways to explain and describe their reasoning, weaknesses, and limitations. In the probing part of the model interpretability research, studies concern individual languages as well as individual linguistic structures. The question arises: are the detected regularities linguistically coherent, or on the contrary, do they dissonate at the typological scale? Moreover, the majority of studies address the inherent set of languages and linguistic structures, leaving the actual typological diversity knowledge out of scope.In this paper, we present and apply the GUI-assisted framework allowing us to easily probe massive amounts of languages for all the morphosyntactic features present in the Universal Dependencies data. We show that reflecting the anglo-centric trend in NLP over the past years, most of the regularities revealed in the mBERT model are typical for the western-European languages. Our framework can be integrated with the existing probing toolboxes, model cards, and leaderboards, allowing practitioners to use and share their familiar probing methods to interpret multilingual models.Thus we propose a toolkit to systematize the multilingual flaws in multilingual models, providing a reproducible experimental setup for 104 languages and 80 morphosyntactic features.

papers.title: Comparing Template-based and Template-free Language Model Probing
papers.research_question: Do model rankings and absolute scores differ between template-based and template-free probing, and do these differences vary between general and domain-specific models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that template-based and template-free probing methods yield different model rankings and scores, and introduces LIPID, a template-free biomedical probing dataset.
papers.conclusion: The choice of probing technique significantly affects the assessment of LMs' knowledge, emphasizing the necessity of employing multiple evaluation methods for a comprehensive understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Template-free and template-based approaches often rank models differently, except for the top domain-specific models.
Scores decrease by up to 42% Acc@1 when comparing parallel template-free and template-based prompts.
Perplexity is negatively correlated with accuracy in the template-free approach, but positively correlated for template-based probing.
Models tend to predict the same answers frequently across prompts for template-based probing, which is less common when employing template-free techniques.
The template-free approach results in a higher lower bound of knowledge and is cheaper to develop.
papers.limitation:
Other reasons for the differences between template-base and template-free probing may exist beyond those analyzed.
The study does not include extremely large models with billions of parameters.
future_direction: More work can be done on evaluating template-free and template-based probing of extremely large models.
papers.abstract: Sagi Shaier, Kevin Bennett, Lawrence Hunter, Katharina von der Wense. Proceedings of the 18th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Neurons Speak in Ranges: Breaking Free from Discrete Neuronal Attribution
papers.research_question: How does polysemanticity in neurons affect discrete neuron-concept attribution, and can activation ranges enable more precise interpretation and manipulation in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuronLens, a range-based framework for neuron interpretation and manipulation, showing that concept-specific activation ranges allow precise attribution and intervention with reduced collateral damage compared to neuron-level masking.
papers.conclusion: Range-based attribution enables more precise interpretability and targeted manipulation in LLMs, overcoming limitations of discrete neuron-to-concept mapping.
papers.key_findings:
Neuronal activations in LLMs form concept-conditioned, Gaussian-like distributions with minimal overlap across concepts.
Polysemantic neurons exhibit distinct activation ranges for different concepts, enabling fine-grained attribution.
Range-based interventions (e.g., activation range masking) effectively suppress target concepts while causing substantially less degradation to auxiliary concepts and overall model performance than full neuron masking.
The method reduces unintended interference on auxiliary concepts by up to 25 percentage points compared to neuron masking in some settings.
Range-based interventions preserve general capabilities, maintaining or improving performance on benchmarks like MMLU with minor increases in perplexity.
papers.abstract: Interpreting the internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for improving their trustworthiness and utility. Prior work has primarily focused on mapping individual neurons to discrete semantic concepts. However, such mappings struggle to handle the inherent polysemanticity in LLMs, where individual neurons encode multiple, distinct concepts. Through a comprehensive analysis of both encoder and decoder-based LLMs across diverse datasets, we observe that even highly salient neurons, identified via various attribution techniques for specific semantic concepts, consistently exhibit polysemantic behavior. Importantly, activation magnitudes for fine-grained concepts follow distinct, often Gaussian-like distributions with minimal overlap. This observation motivates a shift from neuron attribution to range-based interpretation. We hypothesize that interpreting and manipulating neuron activation ranges would enable more precise interpretability and targeted interventions in LLMs. To validate our hypothesis, we introduce NeuronLens, a novel range-based interpretation and manipulation framework that provides a finer view of neuron activation distributions to localize concept attribution within a neuron. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that NeuronLens significantly reduces unintended interference, while maintaining precise manipulation of targeted concepts, outperforming neuron attribution.

papers.title: Learning to Trust Your Feelings: Leveraging Self-awareness in LLMs for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How well can LLMs discern and express their internal knowledge state to mitigate factual hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs can discern their internal knowledge state with high accuracy but often fail to express it, leading to hallucinations. It introduces the RLKF training framework, which uses knowledge feedback via reinforcement learning to improve model factuality and honesty.
papers.conclusion: RLKF is effective in improving the model's utilization of its internal knowledge state, enhancing performance in knowledge and honesty related tasks, and is a promising solution for hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are highly adept at discerning their internal knowledge, with over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing.
DreamCatcher, an automatic hallucination detection tool, achieves 81% agreement with human annotators.
RLKF training enhances the factuality and honesty of LLMs, improving performance on knowledge-based tasks.
RLKF avoids the 'alignment tax' and improves benchmark performance on various tasks.
The reward model can quickly achieve high accuracy by utilizing internal knowledge state.
papers.abstract: We evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to discern and express their internal knowledge state, a key factor in countering factual hallucination and ensuring reliable application of LLMs. We observe a robust self-awareness of internal knowledge state in LLMs, evidenced by over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing. However, LLMs often fail to express their internal knowledge during generation, leading to factual hallucinations. We develop an automated hallucination annotation tool, Dreamcatcher, which merges knowledge probing and consistency checking methods to rank factual preference data. Using knowledge preference as reward, We propose a Reinforcement Learning from Knowledge Feedback (RLKF) training framework, leveraging reinforcement learning to enhance the factuality and honesty of LLMs. Our experiments across multiple models show that RLKF training effectively enhances the ability of models to utilize their internal knowledge state, boosting performance in a variety of knowledge-based and honesty-related tasks.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

papers.title: LLMs model how humans induce logically structured rules
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) model human induction of logically structured rules? Do they provide a good fit to human behavior and do they use similar logical or logic-like operators?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can model human logical rule induction as well as Bayesian probabilistic Language of Thought (pLoT) models, and they may instantiate a novel theoretical account of human logical concepts without built-in logical primitives.
papers.conclusion: LLMs provide a good model of human logical rule induction and may offer a new theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations underlying human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.
papers.key_findings:
Some LLMs (e.g., GPT4, Gemma-7b) achieve human-level accuracy on logical rule induction tasks.
When prompted to explain rules, LLMs sometimes produce rules that use logical operators similar to humans.
Tuning an LLM (Gemma-7b) on human responses yields a better fit to human learning trajectories than tuning on correct answers or than Bayesian pLoT models.
The tuned LLM's high correlation with human data is not just due to learning the rules correctly; it captures human-like learning patterns.
The tuning generalizes to held-out rules and to new rule types (e.g., minority/majority judgments).
papers.limitation:
It is hard to know what the LLM learns when tuning to human responses, and it is hard to fully eliminate the concern that the tuning process is introducing an artifact that increases fit even on withheld exemplars.
The held-out rules share components with seen rules, so generalization might not be fully compositional.
future_direction: Investigate the representations and processes LLMs use for logical rule induction.
Compare LLM-based accounts to human cognitive processes more deeply.
papers.abstract: A central goal of cognitive science is to provide a computationally explicit account of both the structure of the mind and its development: what are the primitive representational building blocks of cognition, what are the rules via which those primitives combine, and where do these primitives and rules come from in the first place? A long-standing debate concerns the adequacy of artificial neural networks as computational models that can answer these questions, in particular in domains related to abstract cognitive function, such as language and logic. This paper argues that recent advances in neural networks -- specifically, the advent of large language models (LLMs) -- represent an important shift in this debate. We test a variety of LLMs on an existing experimental paradigm used for studying the induction of rules formulated over logical concepts. Across four experiments, we find converging empirical evidence that LLMs provide at least as good a fit to human behavior as models that implement a Bayesian probablistic language of thought (pLoT), which have been the best computational models of human behavior on the same task. Moreover, we show that the LLMs make qualitatively different predictions about the nature of the rules that are inferred and deployed in order to complete the task, indicating that the LLM is unlikely to be a mere implementation of the pLoT solution. Based on these results, we argue that LLMs may instantiate a novel theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations necessary to explain human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: CAT-probing: A Metric-based Approach to Interpret How Pre-trained Models for Programming Language Attend Code Structure
papers.research_question: Can we develop a new probing way to evaluate how CodePTMs attend code structure quantitatively?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CAT-probing, a metric-based probing method to quantitatively interpret how Code Pre-trained Models (CodePTMs) attend to code structure by measuring the commonality between attention scores and Abstract Syntax Tree node distances.
papers.conclusion: The proposed CAT-probing method is effective in interpreting how CodePTMs attend to code structure, as demonstrated by experiments on multiple programming languages.
papers.key_findings:
The token types that CodePTMs focus on vary with programming languages and differ from general human programmer perceptions.
The ability of CodePTMs to capture code structure differs across model layers, with middle layers (4-8) playing an important role in transferring general structural knowledge.
CAT-score is effective in evaluating how CodePTMs attend to code structure, showing strong concordance with model performance on code summarization for encoder-only models.
The relative magnitude relationship of CAT-scores (GraphCodeBERT > CodeBERT > RoBERTa) is consistent across layers and programming languages.
UniXcoder, which uses multiple pre-training modes, shows a different attention distribution and CAT-score pattern compared to encoder-only models.
papers.limitation: The adopted probing approaches mainly focus on encoder-only CodePTMs, which could be just one aspect of the inner workings of CodePTMs.
future_direction: Explore more models with encoder-decoder architecture, like CodeT5 and PLBART.
Explore decoder-only networks like GPT-C.
papers.abstract: Code pre-trained models (CodePTMs) have recently demonstrated significant success in code intelligence. To interpret these models, some probing methods have been applied. However, these methods fail to consider the inherent characteristics of codes. In this paper, to address the problem, we propose a novel probing method CAT-probing to quantitatively interpret how CodePTMs attend code structure. We first denoise the input code sequences based on the token types pre-defined by the compilers to filter those tokens whose attention scores are too small. After that, we define a new metric CAT-score to measure the commonality between the token-level attention scores generated in CodePTMs and the pair-wise distances between corresponding AST nodes. The higher the CAT-score, the stronger the ability of CodePTMs to capture code structure. We conduct extensive experiments to integrate CAT-probing with representative CodePTMs for different programming languages. Experimental results show the effectiveness of CAT-probing in CodePTM interpretation. Our codes and data are publicly available at https://github.com/nchen909/CodeAttention.

papers.title: Conceptual structure coheres in human cognition but not in large language models
papers.research_question: Does conceptual structure in large language models cohere across different probing tasks as it does in humans, or do human and LLM conceptual representations differ in robustness?
papers.core_contribution: Human conceptual structure is robust across different tasks and cultures, but large language models exhibit less coherence in conceptual structure across different probing tasks, indicating a lack of a stable conceptual core.
papers.conclusion: Human conceptual structure is robust to differences in task, language, and culture, while contemporary LLMs lack such coherence, highlighting a fundamental difference between human cognition and current machine language models.
papers.key_findings:
Human conceptual structure estimates from three different tasks (feature listing, triadic comparisons, pairwise ratings) are highly coherent (squared Procrustes correlations between 0.72 and 0.96).
LLM conceptual structure estimates vary depending on the probing task; for GPT-3, the squared Procrustes correlations between different task embeddings are lower (e.g., 0.72 between feature listing and triplet, 0.47 between feature listing and pairwise, 0.25 between triplet and pairwise).
LLM conceptual structure from verified feature lists aligns moderately well with human feature norms (squared Procrustes correlation 0.89), but other LLM-derived embeddings align less well.
Chain-of-thought prompting improves alignment with human conceptual structure for some models but does not achieve human-level coherence.
Embeddings from internal representations (e.g., GPT-3 hidden layers, word2vec, CLIP) do not cohere well with each other or with human embeddings.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a constrained set of 30 concepts from two domains; a larger scale study might reveal different results.
The LLM simulations did not employ advanced prompting techniques like tree-of-thought or self-consistency, which might improve coherence.
LLMs lack multimodal sensory experience that humans have, which might affect conceptual organization.
future_direction: Conduct a larger scale study on larger concept sets.
Investigate the use of advanced prompting techniques (e.g., tree-of-thought, self-consistency) to improve conceptual coherence in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Neural network models of language have long been used as a tool for developing hypotheses about conceptual representation in the mind and brain. For many years, such use involved extracting vector-space representations of words and using distances among these to predict or understand human behavior in various semantic tasks. Contemporary large language models (LLMs), however, make it possible to interrogate the latent structure of conceptual representations using experimental methods nearly identical to those commonly used with human participants. The current work utilizes three common techniques borrowed from cognitive psychology to estimate and compare the structure of concepts in humans and a suite of LLMs. In humans, we show that conceptual structure is robust to differences in culture, language, and method of estimation. Structures estimated from LLM behavior, while individually fairly consistent with those estimated from human behavior, vary much more depending upon the particular task used to generate responses--across tasks, estimates of conceptual structure from the very same model cohere less with one another than do human structure estimates. These results highlight an important difference between contemporary LLMs and human cognition, with implications for understanding some fundamental limitations of contemporary machine language.

papers.title: On the Universal Truthfulness Hyperplane Inside LLMs
papers.research_question: Does a universal truthfulness hyperplane exist within LLMs that can distinguish factually correct and incorrect outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing the diversity of training datasets significantly enhances the generalization of truthfulness probes, supporting the hypothesis that a universal truthfulness hyperplane exists within LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The findings support the existence of a universal truthfulness hyperplane in LLMs, offering directions for future research on hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on diverse datasets achieve ~70% cross-task accuracy, outperforming baselines like Self-Eval and Probability.
Attention head outputs are more effective for probing truthfulness than layer residual activations.
Increasing dataset diversity improves generalization more than increasing sample size.
The universal truthfulness hyperplane is more pronounced in advanced models like Mistral-7b and LLaMA2-13b-chat.
Probes trained on single datasets like TruthfulQA fail to generalize out-of-distribution, indicating overfitting.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various fields, hallucination remains a significant challenge. Recent studies have explored hallucinations through the lens of internal representations, proposing mechanisms to decipher LLMs' adherence to facts. However, these approaches often fail to generalize to out-of-distribution data, leading to concerns about whether internal representation patterns reflect fundamental factual awareness, or only overfit spurious correlations on the specific datasets. In this work, we investigate whether a universal truthfulness hyperplane that distinguishes the model's factually correct and incorrect outputs exists within the model. To this end, we scale up the number of training datasets and conduct an extensive evaluation -- we train the truthfulness hyperplane on a diverse collection of over 40 datasets and examine its cross-task, cross-domain, and in-domain generalization. Our results indicate that increasing the diversity of the training datasets significantly enhances the performance in all scenarios, while the volume of data samples plays a less critical role. This finding supports the optimistic hypothesis that a universal truthfulness hyperplane may indeed exist within the model, offering promising directions for future research.

papers.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What does 'linear representation' actually mean in the context of language models, and how can we make sense of geometric notions like cosine similarity and projection in the representation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the linear representation hypothesis using counterfactuals, connects it to linear probing and model steering, and introduces a causal inner product that unifies different notions of linear representation and respects semantic structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper formalizes linear representation and shows that all natural variants of this notion can be unified through a causal inner product, which plays a critical role in enabling interpretation and control of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Concepts are represented as directions in the unembedding space, supporting the linear representation hypothesis.
The proposed causal inner product respects causal separability, making causally separable concepts approximately orthogonal.
The unembedding representation of a concept can be used as a linear probe to predict the concept from context embeddings.
The embedding representation (obtained via the causal inner product) can be used for intervention, steering the model's output towards a target concept.
The Euclidean inner product does not always capture semantic structure, while the causal inner product does.
papers.abstract: Informally, the 'linear representation hypothesis' is the idea that high-level concepts are represented linearly as directions in some representation space. In this paper, we address two closely related questions: What does "linear representation" actually mean? And, how do we make sense of geometric notions (e.g., cosine similarity or projection) in the representation space? To answer these, we use the language of counterfactuals to give two formalizations of "linear representation", one in the output (word) representation space, and one in the input (sentence) space. We then prove these connect to linear probing and model steering, respectively. To make sense of geometric notions, we use the formalization to identify a particular (non-Euclidean) inner product that respects language structure in a sense we make precise. Using this causal inner product, we show how to unify all notions of linear representation. In particular, this allows the construction of probes and steering vectors using counterfactual pairs. Experiments with LLaMA-2 demonstrate the existence of linear representations of concepts, the connection to interpretation and control, and the fundamental role of the choice of inner product.

papers.title: Improving Reasoning Performance in Large Language Models via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: Can reasoning performance in LLMs be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning performance in LLMs can be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference, without any additional training.
papers.conclusion: The experiments indicate that reasoning can in part be understood to be encoded in the residual stream, similarly to how emotional valence or other features are encoded, and can be modulated via representation engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Control vectors derived from contrastive pairs or PCA can improve model performance on inductive, deductive, and mathematical reasoning tasks.
The intervention generalizes across tasks: control vectors from bAbI improve GSM8K performance and vice versa.
The intervention changes the model's internal representations, as evidenced by changes in KL divergence and entropy.
The method requires no additional training and works by adding control vectors to the residual stream during inference.
The optimal scaling factor α varies across models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Limited scope of models (smaller than production-level state-of-the-art models).
The IOI task is relatively simple, which limits the scope of potential errors and the generalizability of findings.
The need for better contrastive pairs for reasoning to optimally derive control vectors.
future_direction: Applying the intervention to much larger models.
Applying the intervention to more general tasks.
Testing different contrastive schemes.
Exploring ways of embedding this methodology into the models.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have resulted in increasingly anthropomorphic language concerning the ability of LLMs to reason. Whether reasoning in LLMs should be understood to be inherently different is, however, widely debated. We propose utilizing a representation engineering approach wherein model activations are read from the residual stream of an LLM when processing a reasoning task. The activations are used to derive a control vector that is applied to the model as an inference-time intervention, modulating the representational space of the model, to improve performance on the specified task. We publish the code for deriving control vectors and analyzing model representations. The method allows us to improve performance on reasoning benchmarks and assess how control vectors influence the final logit distribution of a model via metrics such as KL divergence and entropy. We apply control vectors to Mistral-7B-Instruct and a range of Pythia models on an inductive, a deductive and mathematical reasoning task. We show that an LLM can, to a certain degree, be controlled to improve its perceived reasoning ability by modulating activations.
